title: Church Government - Part 1: Authority and Submission
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson introduces the biblical doctrine of authority and submission as foundational concepts for understanding church government. Pastor Lyro establishes that God has appointed three primary authority structures (family, state, and church) for the good of humanity, each with delegated but limited spheres of authority. The lesson emphasizes that proper authority is exercised in submission to God's higher authority and serves others, not oneself.

transcript:
## God's Love for His Church and the Purpose of This Series

God loves His church. In the last 150 years it has become popular to say that God loves you as an individual, but the predominant teaching of the Bible is that God loves His church. He only loves you because you are a member of that church. We have grown to dismiss the church and think that we can grow and prosper apart from it. We believe the local church, the visible church, is nothing—just another activity that doesn't need to be safeguarded, attended, or participated in. But that is not the case.

Paul says that Christ died for the church and loves His church. Because of that, there is nothing that can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus.

God loves His church and has appointed a government for it. He has told us how His church is to be led and governed. In this series, we are going to consider two major things.

First, a plurality of biblically qualified elders is God's way to shepherd His flock as prescribed in the Scriptures. You see this in the Old and New Testament. God has appointed elders to be the shepherds of the church—not a single man, not something else. There is a plurality of elders, and these elders must be biblically qualified.

Second, God has appointed deacons to assist the elders in dedicating themselves to the ministry of the word and prayer. The primary job of deacons is not to serve you, but to ensure that elders can focus on the ministry of the word and prayer.

This series focuses on ecclesiology—the doctrine of the church—specifically how the church should be governed and led. It is my conviction that the Scriptures clearly teach this. It is not something we have to decide by good and necessary consequences from the Scriptures. It is clearly and directly taught.

## Authority and Submission: Foundational Concepts

Before we discuss church governance, we need to understand the concepts of authority and submission in general. Often, authority is a dirty word for us. It evokes uneasy feelings. We have all been objects of misused authority, and if we are honest, we have all misused whatever authority God has given us.

Yet authority can be misused; it is designed by God for good. Here is a little secret: no one—absolutely no one—lives outside an authority sphere. None of us are independent. None of us are an authority unto ourselves. None of us exist without somebody else over us. Even Jesus Christ, the man, lived under authority.

If you want to live in a place without authority, you will have to leave this creation. In God's creation, you are always under someone's authority, period. We all have to exercise authority and practice submission in one way or another in our lives.

If you want to study more on this subject, I recommend the book *Authority: How Godly Rule Protects the Vulnerable, Strengthens Communities and Promotes Human Flourishing* by Jonathan Lehman. It is a thick book but easy reading.

### What Is Authority?

Authority is more than just power over a group. It includes God-given power, responsibility, servanthood, and leadership. Authority is an attribute of God, and God is infinite, so there is much more to understand about it.

**Authority is God's good creation gift for sharing His rule and glory.** This tells us that authority is essentially good. In Genesis 1:26, God creates humanity and says:

> "Let us make man in our image according to our likeness and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air and over the cattle, over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." (Genesis 1:26)

Authority is part of the creative order that God instituted for us.

**Authority can be Satan's sinister scheme for supplanting God.** In the Garden of Eden, Satan came as a serpent to talk to Eve. In Genesis 3:1, we read:

> "Now the serpent was more cunning than any beast of the field which the Lord God made and he said to the woman, 'Has God indeed said you shall not eat of every tree of the garden?'" (Genesis 3:1)

Satan introduces a question about God's authority and God's word. He says that God is only doing this to keep you from what is good. He does not want you to know all things. He does not want you to be like Him. That is why He is keeping you from this fruit. Right there, Satan schemes to supplant God's authority.

**Authority is Christ's claim to rescue and redeem.** The Great Commission begins with Jesus saying:

> "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth." (Matthew 28:18)

Everywhere else, somebody else can have authority. But in heaven and on earth—in the spiritual and physical realms—Christ has all authority. He uses that authority to redeem His people to Himself.

### What Is Submission?

We should also talk about submission, which has also been given a negative connotation. Yet we all live in submission in one way or another.

Submission means putting oneself underneath authority, giving someone power over you, putting your interests and desires aside for the general good, and following authority. All of these are aspects of submission.

**Submission is the path to growth, authority, and likeness to Jesus.** This definition encompasses what we may not typically think about—doing something for the good of others and thinking of others. These should also fall under the category of authority.

However, **submission is never absolute and always has limits.**

## How Good Authority Works

Good authority is not unaccountable but submits to a higher authority. No matter who you are, you are under authority. You are submitting to something else.

Good authority does not steal life but creates it. Good authority is not unteachable but seeks wisdom. Good authority is neither permissive nor authoritarian but administers discipline. Good authority is not self-protective but bears the cost of serving others.

Human existence is a mixed bag of good authority and bad authority. We are trying to pull out what good authority looks like so we have a model before us as we think about authority, submission, and how the church should be governed and led.

We can see corruption of authority in the fall. Adam, as the federal head of the family and the whole human race, does not take responsibility. Instead, what does he do? He blames God, saying, "The woman that you gave me." How often we are guilty of blaming God for our own sins, stupidity, and bad actions.

## Two Kinds of Authority: Command and Counsel

When we think about authority in action, we need to consider two kinds of authority: authority of command and authority of counsel.

**Authority of command** is "do this or else." If you do not do it, then there is a rightful consequence.

**Authority of counsel** is the authority to give counsel to somebody else. That counsel should be listened to, but this authority does not have the power to punish.

Let us think of five different categories, institutions, and relationships that have authority:

1. **Parents** have authority of command. As children grow, it transitions from authority of command to authority of counsel.

2. **Government** has authority of command. The state is an authority of command.

3. **Military** has authority of command.

4. **Police officers** have authority of command.

5. **Husbands** have authority of counsel. They do not have the authority to punish their wives.

6. **The Church** has authority of command. The church has the authority to tell you that you must do, believe, act, behave, and think in certain ways. This is where we are very weak in understanding.

Our authority relationships are often marked by inner conflict and anguish. Good authority loves, gives, and generally passes out power. It makes proper delegation. But bad authority discourages, cripples, wilts those around it, sucks dry those that are around them, dehumanizes, uses but does not give.

We see this in the church as well. There is good practice of authority, but sometimes leadership fails and practices bad authority. Ultimately, authority is based on God's nature, and the practice of it has been affected by sin.

## Three God-Appointed Authority Structures

God establishes three authority structures, three institutions for the good of humanity.

### The Family

The first institution is the family. It is not established by humans but by God Himself. Look at Genesis 1:26:

> "Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image according to our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air and over the cattle, over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth. So God created man in his own image in the image of God. He created him male and female. He created them. Then God blessed them and God said to them, be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves on the earth.'" (Genesis 1:26-28)

Notice the parallel between exercising dominion and being fruitful. As if one exercises dominion by being fruitful. This primarily involves having many children, but the quality of the children you raise is important as well.

In Genesis 2:21-24:

> "And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam and he slept and he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place. Then the rib which the Lord God had taken from man, he made into a woman and he brought her to the man. And Adam said, 'This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman because she was taken out of man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife and they shall become one flesh.'" (Genesis 2:21-24)

Here we have the institution of the family, the very first created institution, not by humans but by God Himself.

### The State

The second institution is the state. This is generally accepted among Reformed and biblical thinkers about government in general. Genesis 9 marks the beginning of the state as an institution because the power to regulate life is given to the state and to punish crimes.

> "Surely for your lifeblood I would demand a reckoning from the hand of every beast that will require it and from the hand of every man, from the hand of every man's brother, I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds man's blood by man his blood shall be shed for in the image of God he made man." (Genesis 9:5-6)

As you continue reading the Bible, you reach the Mosaic law and see that capital punishment is not implemented by the individual but by the civil government. Remember the cities of refuge to which those who had killed someone could go to be judged.

According to the Bible, the state is to punish evil and praise those who do good. You can read about that in 1 Peter 2:13-17.

### The Visible Church

The third institution established by God for the good of humanity is the church, the visible church. It was established through the Abrahamic covenant.

Before we read this, it is important to define our terms. There are two terms used in theology: invisible church and visible church.

**The invisible church** consists of the regenerate through the ages. There is no time stamp on the invisible church.

**The visible church** is all who profess faith in Christ and their children in a particular moment in time. The visible church exists in its local manifestation. To be part of the visible church—the collection of all who profess Christ and their children—you must be part of a local church. You cannot be part of the visible church without being part of a local church.

In Genesis 15, we see where the covenant with Abraham is mentioned. The important thing here establishes circumcision as a mark of being part of God's people. Before Abraham, people worshiped God. In Genesis 4, there are those who called upon the name of the Lord. Job was a contemporary with Abraham and was worshiping and offering sacrifices. There was that notion of worship. But the people of God had not been organized into a group.

With Abraham, those who profess faith are brought together. Now, to be part of the people of God, you must be part of this particular family, this particular group. You must have a particular mark put upon yourself as circumcision. If you are not circumcised, the chapter says later on that if you are unwilling to be circumcised, you must be cut off from the people. You are not part of the people of God.

Here you have a visible marking, a visible sign—a sacrament—that identifies you with the people of God in the visible church. Here we have the beginning of the institution of the visible church.

These are the three human institutions, all three appointed not by humans but by God for the good of humanity. We could also say that there is a fourth sphere of authority represented by contracts and covenants. In our world, this sphere will show itself in employment and contractual relationships.

## All Authority Belongs to God

To whom all authority belongs? God. All authority belongs to God. God is the only one who can be truly autonomous—self-ruled, self-governed.

One verse you can attach to this concept is Romans 11:36:

> "From him, through him, and to him are all things." (Romans 11:36)

He is the source of all things. He is the means of all things. He is the goal of all things. He is the only one that is that. Jesus says all authority has been given to Him.

Let us turn to Isaiah 43:10:

> God says, "You are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me? Indeed, there is no other rock. I know no one." (Isaiah 43:10)

God is declaring that there is no other God besides Him. He is making the point that there is nobody before Him, nobody after Him.

Go to Isaiah 44:6:

> "I am the king of Israel and his redeemer, the Lord of hosts. I am the first and I am the last. Have we heard that about somebody else in the Bible? Maybe different words in the book of Revelation. The omega or the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end." (Isaiah 44:6)

God is declaring that He is the beginning and the end. There is nothing else besides Him. He is all things.

Verse 7:

> "And who can proclaim as I do? Then let him declare it and set in order for me since I appointed the ancient people. And the things that are coming and shall come, let them show these to them. Do not fear nor be afraid. Have I not told you from the time and declared it? You are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me? Indeed, there's no other rock. I know no one." (Isaiah 44:7)

God says, sure, if there is another God, let him tell you what is going to happen next, or let them tell you what happened before you were around, before the ancients were around. They cannot. That is the implication because He is the one, the only God. He is the one who is all authority.

Satan offered Adam and Eve autonomy. He said, "If you eat of this fruit, you are going to be like God. You are going to know all things. You are going to be able to rule yourself." He was not able to deliver on that promise because humanity by design is theonomous—ruled by God, made to be ruled by God, dependent on God and His law.

All authority belongs to God. And God delegates authority to several spheres of authority. The family, the state, and the church have been delegated specific spheres over which they exercise delegated authority.

When I use the word "sphere," we can use the word "areas" of authority. The state has authority over certain areas. The church has authority over certain areas. The family has authority over certain areas. There are some times where the subjects of authority overlap. For example, the state has some authority over what parents do—the state has the authority to keep parents accountable over some things they do to their children. So there is a little bit of overlap, but mostly these three areas are independent from one another.

## The Authority and Sphere of Each Institution

What is the authority of the state according to the Bible? The state is to punish evil and praise those who do good. That is the biblical job of the state. You can read about that in 1 Peter 2:13-17.

What is the authority of the family? The family is primarily demonstrated in raising children. The apostle says that specifically, speaking to fathers but to all parents in Ephesians 6:4:

> "You fathers do not provoke your children to rest, but bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord." (Ephesians 6:4)

It does not say the church brings the children up. It does not say the state brings the children up. It says fathers bring the children up. In Deuteronomy 6, speaking to parents in general, says you are in charge of the children. It is not the job of the church. It is not the job of the state. It is the family that has the authority to raise their children.

What is the authority of the church? The church has the authority of the keys. They are the ones that admit people into the visible church of God and declare them to be professing believers. They are the ones that also remove them from the fellowship of the church of God. The church has the power of the keys—not the state or the family. You can read more about that in Matthew 16:18-19.

## Delegated Authority Is Not Absolute

When authority is exercised properly—that is, according to the specific sphere appointed by God—that authority is God's authority. To resist it is to resist God Himself. That is true of all areas of authority.

If the government is being the government as appointed by God and you resist it, you are resisting God. If the family is acting like the family is supposed to act and you resist it, you are resisting God. If the church is acting in faithfulness to the Scriptures and you resist the church, you are resisting God Himself. That is important because delegated authority is true authority—it is the authority of God.

Delegated authority is not absolute, though. What do I mean by that? The delegated authority cannot require that you do what God forbids you to do and cannot prohibit you from doing what God requires you to do. The delegated authority also cannot infringe on somebody else's authority.

So the state cannot infringe into the church's authority. The church cannot infringe into the family's authority. The family cannot infringe into the state's authority, and you can figure out all the different combinations as well.

For example, the church does not have the authority to carry out capital punishment because the sword belongs to the sphere of authority of the state. The state cannot mandate that children attend government schools because the education of children falls under the sphere of authority of the family. The family or individual cannot be the ultimate determiner if one is a Christian or not because that belongs to the sphere of authority of the church.

But we do not think that way. How many times have we said, "Oh, I do not think that person is a Christian" when he is a member in good standing of a church? It is not my job as an individual. It is not your job as an individual to determine if somebody is a Christian or not. It is the job of the church. If the church says so, you go with it.

The idea that delegated authority is not absolute is crucial to keep in mind. As Christians, we have recently gone to two opposite poles on this issue, especially when it comes to the state.

One pole is: I am the ultimate decision maker of what I will pay. If I do not like something, I will not do it. If the state tells me to do something and I do not like it, then I am not going to do it.

The other extreme is: Unless the government is telling me explicitly to sin, I must obey it.

Neither of these positions are biblical positions. We are not going to develop that here—that is for lunchtime.

Interestingly, this second pole is not typically followed in terms of the authority of the church. Unless the church is telling me explicitly to sin, I must obey. Most of us do not think that way. You are going to say, "No, pastor, that is not true." Let me give you an example.

We tell you on the authority of God in His word that you must keep the Sabbath day holy. And you do not. Generally, a lot of you do not. So what are you saying? You say, "Ah, I do not have to obey that." That is exactly what you are saying.

On the other hand, when we view the government with the first pole—"I only do what I think I should do under the government"—we do not apply that to our family, do we? Our five-year-old son says, "I am just going to do what I want to do." Usually we do not say, "Oh, I guess that is it. They get to do whatever they want to do." No, we say, "No, I am your father and your mother. You are going to do what I am telling you to do."

So we are very inconsistent in the application of that. We have to be careful that we follow God in those areas.

The individual is under the authority of these God-appointed institutions. We do not like that because we thoroughly believe that we have been given inalienable rights as individuals and that we must seek those as individuals. The idea of life in community is not that important to us. Yet the individual is under the authority of these God-appointed institutions.

We tend to think of the individual as the ultimate, as how he should behave toward these institutions. But the Bible teaches that the individual's general duty is obedience. We are to grieve when we must not obey, when we cannot obey one of God's institutions. Truly, biblically, not being able to obey is a matter of grievance, not rejoicing. Does it make sense to you?

That was not quite the attitude of the church during COVID, was it? The church in general. There was a kind of pride about "We are defying the government." And I think we were wrong in defying the government in the way we did.
